solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Late reply disappointing Oliver?

blocks.note: first meaning: dead, gone, no longer existing
second meaning: what Oliver Twist hears when he famously asks the workhouse master for extra gruel

explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Oliver Twist the starving boy says 'Please, sir, I want some more', and the answer he dreads is NO MORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone late has died and exists no longer, while the phrase is also the flat refusal a hungry orphan would get.

clue.text: Replacement for one off their trolley, possibly: including second announcer

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one element sits within the other

blocks.clueFragment: Replacement for one off their trolley, possibly
blocks.note: a trolley that has lost one of its small wheels needs a fresh one fitted
S is the standard abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: A cryptic note about someone off their trolley being replaced, perhaps by a second radio announcer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off their trolley' means crazy, but here it is read literally: a caster has come off a trolley, so it needs a NEW CASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A newscaster reads the news on radio or television, a specific kind of broadcast presenter.

clue.text: Study features at college

blocks.note: mug is slang for the face, whose features are eyes, nose and mouth
a student in residence at university is said to be up

explanation.surface: A student studying the features of something while at college.
explanation.walkthrough: British usage has students going 'up' to university and being 'up' during term, a convention crosswords use constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: To mug up is British informal for cramming, learning a subject intensively before an exam.

clue.text: Favour old person like me cycling!

indicators.note: to cycle is to go round, so the final letter comes round to the front

blocks.note: O is the usual abbreviation for old
the one speaking in the clue is the compiler, who is a setter

explanation.surface: An elderly setter asks for a favour while out on a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Me' in a clue means the setter. 'Cycling' looks like the old person's hobby, but it moves the last letter R to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A favour in the older sense is a ribbon badge worn to show support, and a rosette is exactly such a knot of ribbon.

clue.text: American eagle acquiring American identifier

indicators.note: to acquire is to take something in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: US abbreviates the United States, so American
the erne is the sea eagle, a crossword favourite
Am is a standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: An American bald eagle being given some kind of US tag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American eagle' reads as one bird, but the words split. The erne, a sea eagle, is a crossword stalwart worth memorising.
explanation.definitionFit: A username is the login handle by which a computer system recognises its account holder, a label that tells users apart.

clue.text: Strongbox not closing after chap’s put in bundle

indicators.note: not closing means lacking the end, so the final letter is dropped
something put in goes inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a safe is a strongbox for valuables
a chap is a man, referred to as he

explanation.surface: A man stuffs a bundle into a safe that will not shut properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Closing' suggests a lid that will not shut, but it means the last letter, which is cut off before the chap goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheaf is a bundle, of corn stalks tied after reaping or of papers held together.

clue.text: Philosopher to take stock of dictator?

indicators.note: someone who dictates speaks words for another to write down, so this is how the word sounds

blocks.note: to rustle is to steal livestock, and stock can mean farm animals

explanation.surface: A philosopher reviewing a tyrant's resources.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take stock' wants to mean assess, but stock here is cattle, and taking it is rustling. A dictator is read as one who dictates, speaking aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertrand Russell was a British logician and thinker, one of the most famous twentieth-century philosophers.

clue.text: Article that has trashed RUC is too shocking

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked and thrown about, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: a is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece attacking the RUC, the old Northern Ireland police force, is deemed too shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: The RUC was the Royal Ulster Constabulary, the police of Northern Ireland until 2001; its letters just join the pile.
explanation.definitionFit: Atrocious describes something appallingly bad or horrifying, a close synonym for what outrages people.

clue.text: Steers away from horse, making for trees

indicators.note: going away from something separates them, so one piece is taken off the other

blocks.note: to helm a vessel is to steer it
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: Cattle wander away from a horse and head for the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steers' looks like young bulls, but it is the verb. Horse is drug slang for heroin, whose symbol is H.
explanation.definitionFit: Elms are tall deciduous hardwoods, a common kind of broadleaf in the British countryside.

clue.text: Port originally consumed by a storyteller in private?

indicators.note: what comes originally is at the start, so only the opening letter counts
something in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the first letter of this word
taken as written
a GI is an American soldier, a private
a storyteller is someone who tells stories, fibs

explanation.surface: Someone privately drinks their port as a raconteur spins a yarn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' wants to be the wine being consumed; it is a harbour city. 'Telling stories' is a euphemism for lying, and GI is the American private soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Cagliari is the capital of Sardinia and a major Mediterranean seaport on its southern coast.

clue.text: Undertakes large welcome for one needing work

blocks.note: to wage a war or campaign is to undertake it
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
ave is the Latin greeting, hail

explanation.surface: Someone takes on a big welcome effort for a jobseeker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undertakes' hides the verb wage, as in waging war; AVE is Latin for hail, used as a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: A wage slave is someone wholly dependent on paid employment to survive, so they must keep working.

clue.text: Beat it with small clubs and hammer

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
C stands for clubs, the card suit
to ram is to hammer or pound

explanation.surface: Someone batters an object using little clubs and a hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat it' looks like an instruction to pound something with the weapons that follow, but it is the slang for go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal commands telling someone to leave at once, the same brusque dismissal in slang.

clue.text: Paris accepting blame ultimately for artist’s murder perhaps

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter is used
to accept one thing for another is to take it in exchange, so a letter swap is made

blocks.note: Paris is the chief city of its country
the final letter of this word
an RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: Paris takes the blame for an artist being killed.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris is CAPITAL OF FRANCE, which accepts E in place of RA. RA, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts, is the usual crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: A capital offence is a crime punishable by death, and murder is the classic example of one.

clue.text: A boy my lord ordered to bring a drink

indicators.note: things ordered are put into an arrangement, so these letters take a new sequence

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An aristocrat tells a page boy to fetch him a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' reads as the lord giving a command, but it is the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bloody Mary is a cocktail of vodka and tomato juice, a classic mixed alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Squash item to consistently overlook or miss?

definitions.note: a miss is a girl or young woman; Susie is one example of a girl's name

indicators.note: overlooking steadily, again and again, means skipping every other letter

blocks.note: take the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: A squash player asks whether to keep ignoring a piece of equipment or just miss the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squash' looks like the racket sport, but it is just fodder, and 'miss' is a young woman, not a failed shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Susie is a girl's name, and a miss is a girl, so the name serves as an example with the question mark.

clue.text: Cow to stand in entrance to field? Half just inside

indicators.note: half means only one of two equal parts, so the rest is cut away
inside means within, so one piece sits in the middle of the other

blocks.note: a sub is a substitute, one who stands in
a field is entered by a gate
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cow stands at a field gate with half her body inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' wants to be the animal at the gate; it is the verb meaning to intimidate. Half of JUST is JU.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to frighten them into submission, and to subjugate is to bring under control by force.

clue.text: One had on the first Apollo short fire, tragically

indicators.note: something short is lacking its end, so the last letter goes
a tragic outcome is a disaster that throws everything into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the word loses its final letter

explanation.surface: It recalls the Apollo 1 cabin fire of 1967, which killed three astronauts.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hides in 'One had on the first': to be had is to be fooled, and the first is 1 April.
explanation.definitionFit: An April fool is a victim of a prank played on the first day of April, someone tricked or taken in.

clue.text: Busy time in game’s doubly hard for us

blocks.note: RU is rugby union, and the apostrophe S adds an S
H for hard, as on pencils, written twice
our means belonging to us

explanation.surface: A demanding stretch in a match proves twice as tough for the team.
explanation.walkthrough: RU for rugby union is a stock crossword game, and H is the pencil-grade mark for hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Rush hour is the peak commuting period when roads and trains are most crowded.

clue.text: Bias seems to corrupt missions

indicators.note: to corrupt something is to spoil its proper form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Prejudice appears to be undermining diplomatic missions abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' fits the surface about bias in diplomacy, but it only asks for the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomatic mission is the office of an ambassador in a foreign country, which is an embassy.

clue.text: Who knows when protests arising, indeed

indicators.note: in a down clue arising means going upward, so these letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: demos are protest marches
ay is an old word for yes

explanation.surface: A shrug about when protests will finally break out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arising' fits protests breaking out, but in a down clue it means reading upward. AY is dialect or archaic yes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someday refers to an unspecified future time, exactly the vague shrug of not knowing the date.

clue.text: Mess up, having altered central feature of spooks’ function?

indicators.note: altering the middle part means one character in the centre is swapped for another

blocks.note: MI5 is the British security service; its central figure 5 is changed to the look-alike letter S
a do is a party or social function

explanation.surface: Someone bungles a spy agency's job by tampering with a central part.
explanation.walkthrough: Spooks are spies, and MI5 is Britain's domestic intelligence agency; the digit 5 turns into the similar-looking letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: To misdo is an old verb for doing something wrongly or badly, so to bungle or botch it.

clue.text: Wimp draws naval officer doing handstand?

indicators.note: someone doing a handstand is upside down, and in a down clue that flips the letter order

blocks.note: to milk is to draw off, as milk from a cow
PO stands for petty officer

explanation.surface: A feeble sailor sketches an officer upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draws' suggests sketching; here it means extracting, as in drawing milk.
explanation.definitionFit: A milksop is a feeble, timid person lacking courage, the same idea as a weakling.

clue.text: Where work is not coming to a stop? Yes and no!

definitions.text: Where work is not coming to a stop? Yes and no!

blocks.clueFragment: Where work is not coming to a stop?
blocks.note: surface reading: a break from work that is not really a break
setter's reading: the driver's job does not stop, and yet he is on leave, never coming to a bus stop in service

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase describes a holiday spent doing much the same as your job. 'Stop' plays on the bus stop a driver still passes.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means leisure time spent doing what one normally does for a living, so a vacation that resembles labour.

clue.text: Material academic omitted from transatlantic flight itinerary?

indicators.note: something omitted is left out, so those letters are removed from the rest

blocks.note: a flight across the Atlantic might run from New York, NY, to London
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A lecturer is dropped from a transatlantic travel plan.
explanation.walkthrough: The itinerary is written NY-LONDON; a don is an Oxbridge academic, removed from the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic fibre and the fabric woven from it, used for stockings, clothing and ropes.

clue.text: Delivered letter promoting area

indicators.note: promoting moves something up, and in a down clue it is lifted out and slotted in higher

blocks.note: delta is the Greek fourth letter
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Someone hands over a letter to advertise a district.
explanation.walkthrough: The A at the foot of DELTA is moved up two places, which suits a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Cards are dealt, handed out to players, so the past tense matches handed over or given out.

clue.text: Priest caught removing clothing

indicators.note: clothing is what goes on the outside, so the outer letters are stripped off

blocks.note: to nab is to catch or arrest

explanation.surface: A cleric is arrested while undressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removing clothing' sounds like the priest disrobing, but it strips the outer letters N and D.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbé is a French title for a cleric or abbot, a man in holy orders.

clue.text: Cried like a kid, ill, having to swallow a tablet

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: bad can mean unwell
taken as written
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet

explanation.surface: A sick child whimpers at having to swallow a pill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child, but a kid is a young goat, which bleats.
explanation.definitionFit: A young goat bleats, and that bleating noise is the sound sheep and goats make.

clue.text: State where in the Vosges one’s intercepting climber

indicators.note: to intercept is to cut in on something, so these letters break into the other

blocks.note: où is French for where, and the Vosges are mountains in France
one is I, and apostrophe S is is
a liana is a woody climbing vine

explanation.surface: Asking where in the Vosges mountains a climber is being stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' suggests a mountaineer in the Vosges, but it is a tropical vine. French où means where.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisiana is one of the fifty US states, on the Gulf of Mexico.

clue.text: All maintenance very onerous? Not all

indicators.note: not all means only part is used, so the letters come from a stretch of the phrase

blocks.note: runs from the last letter of the first word into the next two

explanation.surface: A grumble that upkeep is a heavy burden, though not entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All' at the start and 'Not all' at the end look like a paradox, but one is the definition and the other the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyone means every person, and all can mean the same when used for a whole group of people.

clue.text: Bats on regardless, ultimately inconsistent

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the closing letter is kept
in an across clue, one thing placed on another comes after it, so the first-named piece is sent second

blocks.note: the final letter of this word
bats and potty both mean crazy

explanation.surface: A cricketer keeps batting regardless and is ultimately erratic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats on' suggests a batsman carrying on, but bats is British slang for mad; 'on' puts it after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotty performance is patchy and uneven, good in some places and poor in others.
